The White-winged vampire bat (Diaemus youngii) exhibits a basal metabolic rate of 37.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 37.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that was measured under standard respirometry conditions at a body temperature of 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C]. This relatively low oxygen consumption, recorded from a corrected PNAS table, aligns with the reduced energetic demands often observed in obligate blood-feeders, whose liquid diet minimizes the thermic effect of feeding compared to insectivorous bats. Newborn pups weigh approximately 4.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.8 grams], a neonatal mass that is modest in absolute terms yet represents a substantial investment relative to maternal size, reflecting the altricial state typical of phyllostomid neonates. These precocial newborns emerge from the womb with their eyes open and immediately seek a teat, clinging tightly to the mother's fur as she forages.

Following birth, the mother initiates lactation, and the suckling juvenile undergoes a period of rapid mass gain before reaching nutritional independence. The wet weight at weaning is roughly 17 grams [Wwx = roughly 17 grams], a threshold that marks the transition to a fully blood-based diet obtained through independent foraging. The time since birth at weaning is 30.5 days [tx = 30.5 days], a relatively short lactation period for a bat of this body size, which likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a low-quality diet that limits maternal milk production at a temperature of 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C]. All these developmental milestones were recorded in captive colonies maintained under controlled thermoneutral conditions at 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C], emphasizing the importance of stable thermal environments for consistent growth trajectories in this species.

Sexual maturation in Diaemus youngii follows a protracted developmental schedule compared to many other small bats. Under the same thermoneutral conditions that support growth (31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C]), individuals reach puberty at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth], a duration that approximates one full year of postnatal development. This delayed reproductive activation is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed across vampire bat lineages, where the social complexity of cooperative breeding and the nutritional challenges of a blood-based diet likely select for deferred maturity. Adult females eventually achieve an ultimate wet weight of 40 grams [Wwi = 40 grams], with field records indicating that healthy individuals typically fall within a range of 30 to 45 grams depending on regional prey availability and roosting conditions.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and only one litter produced each year [F_R_i = one litter produced each year], resulting in a maximum reproductive rate of one pup annually. The gestation time necessary to produce that single offspring is approximately 259 days [tg = approximately 259 days], as measured in captive animals kept at 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C]; this extended gestational period, equivalent to roughly eight and a half months, is unusually long for a mammal of just 40 grams and reflects the advanced state of neonatal development at parturition. Comparative data from the closely related common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) indicate a similar gestational duration of eight to nine months, suggesting that prolonged pregnancy is a conserved trait among the desmodontine clade, possibly linked to the physiological demands of supporting a haemophagous gestation.

Longevity records for Diaemus youngii indicate that individuals can survive for up to 20 years [am = up to 20 years] in captivity, under the controlled thermal conditions of 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C] that approximate their natural roost microclimate in Neotropical caves. This lifespan is remarkable for a 40-gram bat and far exceeds the typical 4-to-6-year longevity reported for comparably sized insectivorous species, a discrepancy that appears to correlate with the exceptionally low predation pressure and stable food supply available to haematophagous bats. The combination of late puberty, prolonged gestation, single-pup litters, and extreme longevity positions this species at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum, underscoring the profound influence of dietary specialization on the evolution of life-history strategies in the Phyllostomidae.
